posts.text:
i found "executive mindset" to be the biggest differentiator from people who can use agents super effectively

it comes natural for people who had been an executive of a large org before, but it's counter-intuitive for people who haven't done so

a few examples

1. after you send a prompt, do you stare at the chat to see what the agent is doing?

most agent UX today leads people to do that, but a good executive never watches over an employee's shoulder after they've sent an ask - they are immediately on to the next problem

2. do you rely on chat for important decision making?

"just chat" sounds elegant, but there's a reason company executives rarely rely on plain talking for high stake decisions

instead, they ask the team for documents or presentations. it puts a bit more prep work on the team, but the discussions end up being a lot more efficient

3. when your agent did something wrong, do you curse at it and twist its arms to do it right?

some successful executives actually do that as well, but they also do something else afterwards - figure out what allowed the mistake to happen in the first place, and stop it at its root

4. do you spend all your time carefully examining everything to make sure the code is bug free?

now this is getting spicy, but you can pick any popular product on earth and you won't find a single one that's bug free

good executives accept the calculated risk and invest time in the right workflows to catch bugs early before shipping, get alerts if they happen, and making sure fixes can go out quickly - never make themselves the bottleneck by being the tester

our tools, skills, workflows etc change all the time, but building the right mindset is durable and can help you for a long time

if you aren't clear how to acquire the mindset yet, i recommend starting with asking yourself this when you try to decide to do something or not -

"if i have 100x more agents doing 100x more work for me every day, how would i do this?"

do this enough times, and you'll find yourself actually able to control 100x more agents effectively

posts.text:
overheard from friends talking about AI in China, and it’s very alarming

- AI short films went massive in China market because of how good the video models are now

- the first wave of people who mastered using AI to generate short films and comics made quite some money because they could produce a lot more content than traditional workflows

- but within just a few months, everybody and their mom could make equally good short films because all the expertise could be written in a markdown file

- when everyone’s more productive, no one actually has an advantage and it’s a race to the bottom. very quickly it became impossible to make money, and everyone’s busier than they were without AI

- the only one making money now is companies like bytedance who owns user demand and distribution. they sell ads to creators who pay to get traffic, and eventually ad spend became 80% of those creators’ operating expense, while AI tokens is less than 5%

so what are the problems here? 

1. there’s no moat if you are creating anything with AI

if a human is really good at something, and it’s hard to find more humans who can do the same, they can leverage the scarcity of their skill to get paid very well

but if AI is good at something, it will be infinitely replicated, so there’s no scarcity hence you can’t really expect a sustainable business by creating anything with AI

2. more creators created more content people actually liked. that’s a good thing

but the economical benefit of that all got absorbed by the distribution platforms

there’s a famous chinese poem 遍身罗绮者，不是养蚕人 - it basically says people who dress well aren’t the people making dresses. that’s exactly what’s happening here

if our society doesn’t figure out a better way to distribute wealth, AI will help billionaires become trillionaires while average people become more exhausted than ever

posts.text:
my open source projects collectively crossed 30k+ stars on github, going from almost zero just a few months ago! 🎉

reflecting on the journey, here are some learnings about growing and maintaining open source projects:

1. make videos sharing your OSS projects

videos, not tweets. this is probably my most important tip

i had a few viral tweets introducing my OSS projects that got lucky and had hundreds of thousands of views, but what brought in way more serious users and contributors was my youtube videos

good videos take a lot more effort to make, but it gives people a much more direct understanding of how your project works and how it delivers value. my hero project firstmate https://github.com/kunchenguid/firstmate grew largely due to my video content

make some videos. and make some more

2. use open source as a super power

i can't overstate how much better the tools got because of open source contributions from others. people bring great ideas, and test + fix the product in all kinds of edge cases that i can't possibly discover

in a way, an OSS product can guide itself towards PMF, because the community would collectively steer it towards the right direction

now that even non-developers can participate in contributing to OSS, this super power is becoming even stronger

3. set a minimum bar on contribution quality

the super power can also be a double edged sword here. especially with AI which allowed a lot more people to contribute but also lowered the bar. if left unchecked, you get a lot of noise

some projects outright disabled all PRs, while some others refuse to take anything done with AI. neither of which is the right approach IMO

my solution has been to raise the minimum bar by requiring all contributions to be raised through no-mistakes. it enforces a level of rigor, and slightly increases the cost to contribute so low quality noise would often shy away

i have a github action for enforcing this - https://github.com/kunchenguid/no-mistakes/tree/main/.github/actions/require-no-mistakes which you can use for your projects too

4. automate as much maintenance as possible

if you've contributed to my repos, you might have seen some of my automation at work. here's an example - https://github.com/kunchenguid/runner-up/pull/52 

i receive dozens, sometimes hundreds of incoming issues + PRs every day across my repos - i can't imagine how i could have kept all these projects moving if i hadn't leveraged agents to automate the triage work

i run the automation in grok bot with my firstmate bot there https://x.ai/bot/__4FfrkUdvpdMk6-LKg5r - it can set up a different bot per each repo, and creates the routines to triage incoming issues and PRs using cursor cloud agents according to my rules, yet allows me to talk to just the firstmate about everything

an important pre-requisite to doing that is a good documented vision for your project, which i write using https://github.com/kunchenguid/vision - with a clearly written vision statement, your triage agents can automatically rule out changes that don't align, and focus on the ones that would further the project towards the direction you want

working with AI is fundamentally asking someone else to produce the work you want

we spend a lot of time communicating context, goals, giving feedback, setting rewards, shaping workflows and SOPs. it’s a managerial experience

i’ve always felt a bit sad about that, because it took away the experience and joy of being a pure craftsman that produces great work directly

chopin can’t be chopin by hiring a team and telling his employees to compose for him. these masterpieces had to be created by a craftsman directly, and i think many of us humans deep down seek that mastery and joy

when the world gets filled with more and more agents and robots, every human’s job becomes an agent manager

are we sure that’s what we want?

i’ve been trying to get rid of adversarial reviews for quite a while now, but unfortunately every time i stopped it, i would find myself simply delaying the discovery of real problems, and the later i find them the more they cost

as a data point, i had measured how many real problems my adversarial reviewers actually caught, and it’s a lot.. 

that said, a good adversarial review setup is necessary for the ROI to be justifiable. i think a few things are very important:

1. original user intent must be explicitly collected (usually can be found in session transcripts where user inputs are) and passed to the reviewers 

2. there needs to be a human in the loop for ambiguous decisions. any scope change / expansion needs to escalated to the human user for decision

3. reviewers need to treat complexity like a disease and actively point out simplification opportunities 

4. reviewers need to challenge the lack of empirical evidence and hold the implementer accountable to prove their change

For 9 weeks, I mostly talked to one AI chat.
⠀
In that time, it finished 560+ tasks and merged 365 pull requests across my projects.
⠀
Yesterday, at Builder Sundays hosted at @Shopify's Ottawa office, I showed how. The tool is @myfirstmate, a free, open-source project by @kunchenguid, a former L8 engineer at Atlassian.
⠀
Kun built it because juggling parallel agent sessions was killing his focus. Every switch meant remembering what that session was about and what to do next. He didn't want a smarter workflow. He wanted the calm back, and the confidence that nothing falls through the cracks when you look away.
⠀
How it works: you are the captain, one agent acts as your firstmate, and a crew of agents does the work. Nothing goes live without your yes.
⠀
→ Orchestration. I only talk to firstmate. It breaks the work into separate tasks, starts a dedicated agent session for each one, and runs them in parallel. It keeps an eye on every session, handles the small stuff itself, and only comes to me when a decision actually needs me. When a task is done, it brings the result back for my review and approval.
⠀
→ Memory. It keeps my projects, rules and in-flight work. /bearings is my morning brief, /stow saves what it learned. I close the laptop and pick up tomorrow where I left off.
⠀
→ It improves itself. If something isn't working, I ask firstmate, and it fixes itself.
⠀
The result: Partexia went live on iOS and Android, and CrewTower shipped 23 releases.

Thank you Kun Chen for building this and sharing it with everyone.

posts.text:
been testing the new multiplexer Rex for a while, and my feelings are very mixed

tl;dr i think i'll stick with herdr for now

while it's a beautifully designed app, i couldn't quite find any real reason yet to prefer Rex other than it being beautiful

biggest sticking point is that it's a middle ground between GUI and TUI. with a full on GUI like t3code we get rich visuals and interactions. with a full on TUI like tmux and herdr we get pure keyboard interaction and can run it from any ssh client consistently

with Rex i get neither of that. and i have to use Rex everywhere or otherwise i'm locked out of my own work. if i'm going to abandon some of the benefits of full TUI over simple ssh, i'd probably just go full GUI at that point, instead of locking my terminal sessions behind another GUI app

this also makes me question the new herdr app, because it seems to be heading in the same direction as Rex. they will both end up competing with other GUI apps without the strength of being a real terminal program

i hope herdr TUI stays because that's still my favorite. perhaps turn it into a client for herdr-core so people can choose to access the same sessions from either a GUI or a TUI?
